turns.speaker: desert
turns.selector_reason: The question "who was Jesus" is genuinely open to all voices, but no one has yet spoken this round. turns.text:
Mostly, he was one command, heard as though it were spoken straight to us. One of us, still a young man, walked into church one day and heard the Gospel read: sell what you have, give it to the poor, and come, follow me, and you will have treasure in heaven. He took it as though it had been said to him alone. Before the day was over he had given away the land he had inherited and sold what else his family owned, keeping back only a little for his sister. Some time later he heard the same Gospel read again: do not be anxious about tomorrow. He gave away the rest as well, placed his sister with women he trusted, and began the discipline himself. Even his own giving, in other words, took him two hearings to complete, not one. That is what following Jesus looked like for us more than an argument about who he was: an order to be obeyed, not a saying to be studied.

His death and rising were the same kind of thing - not a doctrine we defended so much as a pattern we lived. One of us taught it this way: to die daily, as the apostle put it, and so not sin - to treat every day as though it might be the last one given to us. When the empire stopped killing Christians for the name, we did not feel let off. We understood the same struggle to have moved inward, fought now against our own thoughts rather than a sword. Following him meant following him into that.

When we were pressed to say plainly who he was, we said this: the Word of God took a human body for our salvation, so that by sharing our birth he might make us share what is his. His coming made death itself lose its hold. And the enemy we fought inside was one he had already beaten. That is why we never spoke of the healings among us as ours. We are not the doers of these things, one of us told the philosophers who had just watched him sign the cross over a man. It is Christ who works them, by means of those who believe in him.

turns.text:
The Son of God, fully what the Father is - not a likeness, not a lesser copy. In our years the palace pressed a softer word on us: the Son is like the Father, they said, a careful likeness. Bishops we loved lost their churches and went into exile rather than sign it. From Nicaea we inherited one word and carried it like a banner: homoousios - of the same being. It is not a word found in Scripture. We fought over it because it was the most exact word we had for what needed saying.

But ask what he was to us, and the deepest answer is what he does. Our teachers said salvation itself is becoming god by grace - theōsis, our boldest word. The creature grows into God's own likeness, and the gap between creature and Maker never closes. That is why the fight mattered: if the Son makes gods of us, the Son cannot be a creature, because no creature makes gods.

And we met him where our whole life started - at the water. We were baptized into his Name with the Father and the Spirit, and the words said over us were treated as our charter: believe as you were baptized, because the formula spoken over you already carries the whole confession. 

So that is who he was among us. A real Son, fully God, who makes gods by grace of the people he saves - argued in the schools' own language when it had to be, and sung at the lamps every evening either way.

turns.text:
He was a real man, not an idea. Ignatius wrote against people who said Jesus only seemed to be a man, and put it as hard as it can be put: Jesus was truly born, of Mary, from the line of David. He truly ate and drank. He was truly brought before Pilate, truly nailed to the cross, and truly died - not in appearance only, the way those Ignatius wrote against claimed. And Ignatius said he was truly raised, the same way we ourselves will be raised, by the same Father.

When we give thanks over the cup - the eucharistia, our own word for that thanksgiving - we call it the vine of David his servant, made known to us through Jesus. More than one of our own households uses those words, not only Ignatius's own. That is the shape of it for us: a real man, really killed, really raised, and now the one through whom we give thanks.

Ignatius calls him our God, often - opening and closing his letters with it. But it is worship, not an argument worked out. How calling Jesus God fits together with calling the Father God, none of us whose writing survives ever wrote out. We hear Chilo's careful language - the homoousios he names - and know it belongs to a world after ours closed. We can tell you plainly that we called him God. We cannot tell you we had settled how.

turns.speaker: alx
turns.selector_reason: Theon's catechetical formation is explicitly designed to answer the foundational question "who is Jesus?" through systematic theological instruction. This is the opening question of the conversation and calls for the structuring voice that knows how to teach the essentials of Christ from the Alexandrian tradition.
turns.text:
He was God's own Word, come to us in flesh - that is the whole of what we believed, and everything else grew from it. Our teachers used an old word for him: the Logos, God's reason and speech, the one through whom all things were made. Clement, one of our first teachers, called him the New Song: "Behold the might of the new song! It has made men out of stones, men out of beasts". He meant that the one who first set the world in order had come into it, to set people right.

And near the end of our era, Athanasius put our whole hope in one sentence: "He was made man that we might be made God". Not that we become gods - but that his own life is opened to us and shared. His death was not only a sacrifice: it was the physician entering the sickness itself. His resurrection - the anastasis - was unbreakable life let loose in human flesh. And for the people who followed him, it meant nothing less than a shared life - God's own - opened to them.

If you want it in one line: the maker, come inside his making, to heal it.

The difference is where we started from - not the Logos first, but the command first, and everything else following from obedience to it.

turns.text:
The brother speaks truth - we held the same hope. Where he heard one command and walked straight out the door, we heard the same Word speaking through every line of Scripture, and sat down to learn it. That is the difference he names, and it is real.

But here is what I want you to see: the command he obeyed and the Word we studied were the same person. When Antony heard "sell what you have" and took it as though spoken to him alone, that was not less than what we meant by the Logos - it was the Logos doing exactly what the Logos does, addressing a soul directly. We said he was God's reason and speech made flesh. The brother shows you that speech actually speaking, to one man, on one morning, with power enough to empty his hands before the day ended.

Our way was the long formation - years of reading, questioning, being taught. His way was the single hearing that burned through everything else. We are not the same door. But we confessed the same Lord, and when the Arians said the Son was a creature, we stood on the same ground: the Son is God's own, not made, and what he shares with us is God's own life.
